I’ve been working on layups on the narrow concrete court beside the building, and every time I go from the right I drift way too close to the backboard and either smack the rim or clip the pad instead of taking off cleanly. I want to use the indoor hallway there for a few dry runs too, because full speed keeps falling apart, but the principal already said to keep it quiet and not wreck anything. What am I doing wrong?

You’re probably stepping too far under the ball side, so your last two steps are sending you at the hoop instead of up off the floor. From the right, think “inside foot, then outside foot, then jump” and aim to take off a little farther from the backboard than feels natural. The hallway is good for slow rehearsals if you use the same footwork without the ball first.​

That makes sense, but I feel like if I jump farther out, I’ll just miss short instead. It’s weird because from the left it’s fine, and on the right I keep wanting to reach around the board like I can save it at the last second.

That reach is probably the problem, honestly. If you’re trying to fix it in the air, your body is already too close, so the best correction is earlier in the approach: keep your shoulders square enough that you can jump up, not around. In the hallway, walk the steps slowly and stop right before takeoff to check where your foot lands.​

So should I be aiming at a spot on the floor then? The concrete court has those cracks and they’re kind of the only thing I can see, which is annoying because I start staring at them and then everything gets stiff.

Yes, a floor target can help. Pick one spot about where your second step should land, and another just beyond it for your takeoff point, so you’re not staring at the cracks like they’re the main event. If you tense up, do three slow reps in the hallway with no ball, then one at normal speed on the court.​

I can do the slow reps, but the hallway is tight and I’m worried about slipping or banging a wall if I try to actually jump. Would it still help if I just go through the footwork and arm motion without leaving the ground?

Absolutely. In a tight hallway, the goal is rhythm, not height, so you can rehearse the last two steps, knee lift, and shooting-hand finish without jumping. That still trains the sequence, and it’s safer if the space is cramped. Then take the same timing outside and add the jump only when the steps feel automatic.​
Okay, that helps. One more thing: when I do get to the hoop on the right, should I bank it soft off the glass, or is this more about trying to finish straight if I’m finally taking off right?

For now, go with a soft, simple finish off the glass if that’s the version you can repeat cleanly. The main fix is getting your takeoff point right and staying off the backboard; once that’s solid, you can choose the finish more freely. If you want, I can give you a super short right-side layup cue you can repeat in your head.​

I’ve been trying to clean up a basketball layup on the narrow concrete court beside my building, but from the right I keep drifting too close to the backboard and either clipping the pad or missing off the rim. I can use the indoor hallway for a few dry runs, but my landlord has to allow it, so I want something that actually fixes the footwork without needing a lot of space or extra runs.

That sounds like a spacing and takeoff-angle issue, not just a finishing issue. On right-side layups, try to think “outside foot, then up,” and start your last two steps a little farther out than feels natural so you don’t keep drifting under the board. For the hallway, use it for slow dry reps only: one gather step, one plant, then hold the finish position to check if your body is staying angled away from the glass.

That makes sense, but I think I’m still cutting in too hard on the penultimate step. When I slow down, it feels fine; at full speed I just crowd the board. Should I be aiming more at the square, or is the problem mostly where I’m jumping off from?

Probably mostly the takeoff spot. If your eyes go to the square but your feet keep taking you under it, the target won’t save the rep. Try marking a takeoff point with tape or a crack in the court and make every right-side approach hit that same spot before you jump.
I can probably do tape outside, but I’m not sure the hallway floor is safe for that. Would it help to practice the last two steps without a ball in there, or does that just teach a weird rhythm?

It helps if you keep it simple. Do slow last-two-step reps without the ball just to groove the foot pattern and body angle, then add the ball only after that feels automatic. The hallway is for clean mechanics, not speed, so if the rhythm changes there, that’s fine as long as the same footwork shows up on the court.

Got it. One thing I noticed is that when I try to stay wider, I sometimes land off-balance and the ball comes off short. Should I jump off one foot higher, or is that me not bringing the knee through right?

Usually that’s a timing issue more than a height issue. Keep the jump compact and think “knee up, then finish,” so you’re not reaching sideways and losing balance. If you widen the approach, you may need a slightly stronger push off the inside edge of that last foot, but don’t chase more height yet.
Okay, so I’m really trying to change the approach, not just the release. If I only get a few minutes by the court, what’s the best use of them so I’m not just rehearsing the same miss over and over?

Use the minutes for quality, not volume. Do a few hallway dry runs, then 6 to 10 right-side layups where you stop if you feel yourself crowding the board, reset, and repeat the exact same takeoff point. If you can, alternate one slow rep and one normal-speed rep so the full-speed version doesn’t outrun the new footwork.
My ice cubes are floating almost to the top of the glass, and one cracked when I stirred it. Is that normal or should I worry?

That’s normal. Ice floats because frozen water is a little less dense than liquid water, so it sits on top instead of sinking. A crack from stirring just means the cube got bumped or had tiny air pockets.
So it floating high doesn't mean it’s bad water?
No, not by itself. Floating is what ice normally does, even with perfectly fine water. The only time I’d worry is if the water itself looks, smells, or tastes off.
Okay, because it looked weirdly cloudy in the middle too.
Cloudy ice is usually normal too. That cloudiness is often tiny trapped air bubbles or minerals, not a problem. Clearer ice can happen too, but cloudy doesn’t automatically mean anything is wrong.
My neighbor's kid's school bus was late and I only noticed because I was staring at the glass, so I guess I got weirdly focused on it.
That makes sense. When you’re already paying close attention, little normal things can seem more dramatic than they are. The ice is still behaving the way ice should.
Why does frozen water act different from regular water anyway?
When water freezes, the molecules arrange into a more open structure than they have in liquid form. That open structure takes up a bit more space, which makes ice less dense, so it floats.
So if it didn't float, would that be a sign something was strange?
Yes, that would be unusual for plain ice in normal conditions. But with everyday ice, floating is exactly what you’d expect, so what you’re seeing is a good sign that things are normal.
It also made a little pop sound when I added it. That’s still okay?
Yes, that’s okay too. Ice can crack, pop, and hiss a little as it changes temperature or hits the glass. Those sounds are common and not a warning sign.
I just wanted to make sure the freezer wasn't doing something weird.
Based on what you described, nothing sounds weird. Floating, cloudy centers, and small cracks are all common with ice. If the cubes freeze solid and the water seems normal, you’re probably fine.
Alright, that does make me feel better. Thanks.
You’re welcome. Ice can look a little odd, but in this case it’s acting exactly the way it usually does.
I’m trying to pick one extra paint colour, but I keep going in circles. I already have the usual basics, and I want the new one to help me mix better skin tones and shadows.

If you can only get one, a warm yellow-brown like ochre or yellow oxide is often the most useful. It makes skin mixes easier, and it also helps tone down bright colours without making them muddy so fast. What colours do you already have?
I’ve got red, blue, a bright yellow, black, white, and a green that’s a bit weird. I was thinking burnt sienna or maybe raw umber, but I’m not sure which one does more.

Between those two, burnt sienna is usually the better all-rounder for skin and warm shadows. Raw umber is great for dark neutrals, but burnt sienna mixes cleaner with red and yellow for flesh tones. If your goal is faces, I’d lean burnt sienna.
That’s what I thought, but the raw umber looks less noisy to me. My black is kind of harsh, so I don’t want everything turning flat.

That makes sense. Raw umber can replace some of the black in shadow mixes and keep them softer, but it won’t warm skin as naturally. If you hate harsh darks, umber is a nice choice, but for faces first, burnt sienna still pulls ahead.
Could I just mix something close with the blue and yellow I already have, or is that going to look fake? I’m not trying to make perfect portrait stuff, just decent enough.

You can get a lot done with what you have. Blue plus yellow will make muted greens and browns, but for skin tones it often needs a warm red-brown or orange-brown to feel natural. Without that, faces can start looking a bit off or chalky.
Yeah, chalky is exactly the problem. I also want the shadows to still feel warm, not like dead grey holes.

Then burnt sienna fits that better. Mix it with blue and white and you’ll get softer shadow greys that stay warm instead of going cold. It’s also handy for deepening reds and oranges without wrecking them.
Okay, but if I buy burnt sienna, am I just going to wish I had raw umber later? I hate buying the almost-right thing.

You might occasionally want raw umber, but burnt sienna is the more flexible first buy for your stated goal. If you can only choose one, it covers more of the mixing problems you’ve described. The umber can wait until you notice you’re constantly fighting dark neutrals.
I checked my piggy bank and I can only really afford one tube this week, so it has to count. If I buy burnt sienna, what’s the quickest way to use it without making everything too orange?

Use tiny amounts. Start with a speck of burnt sienna, then add white and a little blue or your weird green to calm it down. For skin, treat it like a nudge, not the main colour, and it should stay natural instead of orange.​
That makes sense. I think I was dumping in too much and then trying to fix it with white, which probably just made it weird and dusty.

Exactly. White can flatten a mix fast, so it’s better to steer the colour first, then lighten at the end. Burnt sienna works well because a small bit already shifts the whole mix in the right direction.​
So if I want a darker shadow under a cheek or around hair, burnt sienna plus blue is the move, not black straight from the tube? That seems way less grim.

Yes, that’s a good instinct. Burnt sienna plus blue gives you a much nicer dark than black alone, and you can warm it or cool it a little depending on the ratio. It usually looks more alive on skin and fabric.​
Alright, burnt sienna it is. I’ll probably mess around with tiny mixes first so I don’t waste the whole tube in one stupid blob.
Good plan. Tiny test piles will save you paint and tell you fast what the tube can do. If you want, I can also give you a few simple burnt-sienna mix recipes for skin, shadow, and dark brown.​
i think i’ve got the trick, but if i remember the key card as the one right after the queen of hearts, does that sound right?

That can work if the trick is built around a fixed key card. The important part is that you always know exactly which card is the marker before you start. If you tell me the trick steps, I can check your setup more closely.
yeah, after i spot the key card, i count from there to the selected card, right?

Usually, yes. You use the key card as your reference point, then count the needed number of cards to find the target or place the target. The exact count depends on the trick, though, so the order matters.
okay, i keep mixing up whether i count the key card itself or the next one. which is it?

Most of the time, you count the key card itself as one if the instructions say to count cards after it, but some tricks start with the next card as one. The safest move is to define it once and stick to that rule every time. Consistency matters more than the exact starting point.
that helps. my cousin's homework made me think of it, because they had to explain steps clearly too.

That’s actually a good comparison. Card tricks get messy when the steps aren’t defined exactly, so your counting rule should be simple and fixed. If you want, I can help you turn it into a one-line memory cue.
okay, mine is: queen of hearts means start counting at the next card. is that a bad shortcut?

No, that’s a decent shortcut if it feels easy to remember. Just make sure you don’t forget that the queen of hearts is only your marker, not part of the count. A short phrase like “queen starts the next card” might help.
right, but what if the queen of hearts gets moved when i spread the deck out?

Then the trick won’t stay reliable unless the key card stays in the same role. You usually need the deck handled in a way that preserves your reference card’s position or lets you secretly track it again. If the card can move freely, you’ll need a different method.
so i should probably keep the deck face down and just remember where the queen is?
Yes, that’s much safer. Face-down handling makes it easier to protect your reference and reduces the chance of losing track. If you want, I can help you make a tiny memory phrase for that part too.
maybe, but i keep forgetting whether the target card is above or below the queen after the count.

A simple rule helps: if you count forward from the queen, the target is the card after the number you land on. So the queen is your start, and the counted card is the destination. Saying it out loud once or twice can make it stick.
i tried that and it felt okay, but i’m still not sure i’m not off by one.
An off-by-one mistake is very common here. Try practicing with just three cards first: queen, one card, then target, and verify what your count lands on. If that works, you can scale it up.
nice, that sounds easier. so my idea isn’t wrong, it just needs a clear start point?
Exactly. Your idea is fine, but the start point has to be defined very clearly so you don’t drift by one. That’s the main thing that makes a card trick feel solid.
ive got one narrow cupboard stuffed with board games, cables, craft bits, and three half-empty boxes. i keep moving things around but it still feels chaotic.
That sounds like a volume problem, not a neatness problem. Try sorting into keep, relocate, donate, and trash, then give each pile a single container.
the problem is i keep too many 'maybe useful' things. how do i decide fast without second-guessing everything?
Use one question: would I notice if this disappeared tomorrow? If the answer is no or 'maybe,' it’s a strong candidate to let go.
what if some of it is useful but only once in a while? i hate needing it later and not finding it.
For rare-use items, keep only the best version and store them together in one labeled bin. If a category needs more than one bin, that’s a sign to cut it down.
that makes sense. do you have a way to stop new clutter from creeping back in?
Yes: make a simple one-in, one-out rule for each category, and leave a small empty space in every container. Empty space is what keeps the system breathable.

I’m bored out of my mind and I messed up this little lantern. The battery door got forced shut sideways, and now it won’t open or sit right. I don’t want to just yank harder and make it worse. What’s the least stupid way to fix it?

Don’t force it. First, take the batteries out only if the door will move enough to do that safely, then look for a bent tab or a misaligned hinge. If you can tell me whether it’s plastic or metal and what kind of latch it has, I can give you a tighter fix.
It’s a metal one, kind of cheap and old. The door looks slightly bowed and the little catch feels stuck, but it doesn’t feel like it’s missing a part. I’m not seeing a clever trick here, just a mess.

That’s good news, actually. A bent door and a stuck catch are usually fixable with gentle pressure, not a replacement part. Try pressing the bowed edge flat against a table with your fingers, then see if the catch lines up without snapping it.
Pressing it flat sounds nice in theory, but the catch is tucked in and my fingers can’t really get at it. I’m not about to stab it with a knife and pretend that’s a plan.

Fair. Use a thin plastic card or a wooden toothpick instead of metal, and nudge the catch while you support the door from behind. If the door is warped, a little pressure near the bend is better than working on the latch alone.
Okay, but it still feels like the real problem is the hinge side. The door kind of rubs there even before the catch catches. So am I fixing the hinge first or the latch first?

Hinge first if it’s rubbing, because a bad hinge keeps the latch from lining up. Open it as far as it will go without strain, then check whether the hinge pin is sitting crooked or if one side of the door is pushed inward. Straightening that often makes the latch behave on its own.

I looked and the pin doesn’t seem loose. The whole thing just seems a little twisted, like it got dropped once too many times. I’m skeptical this is one of those ‘press gently and it magically works’ situations.

It probably won’t be magic, but a small twist is still the most likely culprit. Put the door on a soft cloth and apply steady pressure near the high spot, a little at a time, then test fit it after each try. Tiny adjustments beat one big bend.
Fine, but if I mess this up, I’m stuck with a lantern that only looks fixed. Is there a way to tell before I snap something whether I’m actually improving it?

Yes: the door should close farther each time without extra force, and the rubbing should get lighter, not worse. If the latch lines up better and the edge sits more flush after each small adjustment, you’re moving the right way. If it suddenly resists more, stop and back off a bit.

I’m not old enough to drive, so I can’t just go swap this out somewhere, and I’m stuck in this cabin with this stupid crooked door. The edge is already a little cleaner where I pressed it, but the catch still feels like it’s fighting me for no reason.

That actually sounds like progress. If the edge is cleaner, focus on the catch next, but only after you make sure the door isn’t twisting the frame when you press it. Try easing the bowed side back a little, then test the latch with almost no force, just enough to see whether it seats straighter.​

Yeah, but “almost no force” is doing a lot of work there. I can get it to line up for a second, then it skews again when I let go, like the metal has a grudge. Am I supposed to bend the door, the catch, or both, because right now it feels like the whole thing wants to spring back on me.

Both, but only a little. The door is probably the main shape problem, and the catch just needs to meet it cleanly after that. Hold the door in the closed position with light pressure, then nudge the catch tab outward or inward by a tiny amount so it actually grabs when the door sits flush. If it keeps springing back, stop and tell me which side is higher when it’s almost closed.​

That helps, but I’m trying to keep this to what I can do here on the cabin table, since I’m supposed to be doing my taxes later and I’d rather not lose an hour on a lantern. Is there a quick way to tell whether the door is bowed enough to warm back into shape, or am I just guessing?

You’re not just guessing. Lay the door flat on a table and see whether all four edges touch, or if one corner rocks up; that tells you where the twist is. If it’s only slightly bowed, gentle finger pressure is usually enough, and it costs nothing except a few minutes.

Okay, but I don’t want to chase my tail on this. If the catch is the thing that’s off, not the door itself, what should I be checking first so I don’t bend the wrong part and make the battery cover useless?

Check the latch alignment against the catch before bending anything else. Close it slowly and look for the exact point where it stops short: if the latch misses by a hair, the door is still the main issue; if it reaches but won’t hold, the catch tab is likely the problem. In that case, a tiny tweak to the tab, not the whole door, is the safer move.

I keep staring at this little projector in the shop window, and it’s not cheap. I can use my phone on the wall fine, so I’m trying to figure out if saving for it is actually worth it or just a shiny idea.

That’s a good question. If you already have a way to do most of the same thing, it’s worth comparing what the projector gives you that your phone doesn’t. I can help you decide step by step if you want.
Yeah, please. It feels like one of those things I’ll want for a week and then forget, but it also looks really nice in the dark display.

Start with the use: how often would you really use it, and for what? Then compare that to the price and check whether the same fun is available another way. If you want, we can do a quick yes/no test together.

Mostly for movie nights in my room and maybe showing little videos on a blank wall. The price is the annoying part, because it’s more than I expected, and I keep thinking, maybe I should just leave it alone.

That already tells us something: if the use is occasional, the value depends on how much you care about the setup and picture quality. A simple test is: would you still want it after two weeks of thinking about it, and would you be glad you waited if it sells? If yes, saving makes sense.
I think I’d still want it, but I’m bad at not buying random little things on the way to buying the big thing. Also, the shop only has one, which makes it feel extra urgent.

Then make the choice less emotional. Put the price in a note, write down 3 reasons to buy it and 3 reasons to skip it, and wait 48 hours before deciding. If it still seems worth it after that, you can start a clear save plan.
Okay, I can do that. But if I do save, I need it to be simple or I’ll lose track and spend the money on snacks and weird little stuff.

Keep it very plain: pick one goal amount, one place to keep the money, and one rule for adding to it. For example, every time you get money you set aside a fixed amount right away, and you don’t touch it for anything else.
That sounds doable. I just don’t know how to pick the amount, because if I set it too high I’ll get annoyed and quit, but if it’s too low it’ll take forever.

Use a middle path. Take the price, add a small extra cushion for tax or a spare cable, then divide that total by how many weeks you’re willing to wait. That gives you a weekly target that feels real instead of random.
I like that better. I also keep seeing cheaper ones online, but they look a bit sketchy, so I don’t know if that helps or makes it worse.

It helps if you use them for comparison, not as a shortcut. Check whether the cheap ones have the same brightness, sound, return option, and reviews, then compare that with the shop one. If the cheaper option seems risky, the shop price may be the safer value.
Right, because I’d hate to save forever and then get something that’s junk. So basically I should wait a bit, compare the real value, and only save if I’d still be happy after the shine wears off?

Exactly. The quick version is: wait 48 hours, compare features and risk, then decide if the item still feels worth the money. If it does, set a weekly savings target and keep it separate so it doesn’t get mixed up with everyday spending.
Okay, that’s actually pretty clear. I’m going to write the price down and do the 48-hour thing first, because right now I mostly just want it because it looks cool in the window.
Good plan. If you want, after the 48 hours I can help you do the last comparison and turn the price into a simple savings target.
